title: Alpine Linux Users Urged to Patch OpenSSH Authentication Flaw
gist: CVE-2026-123158 (*sshole) lets unauthenticated attackers log into passwordless accounts on OpenSSH builds using musl without PAM by sending passwords over 256 bytes; Alpine Linux, including its default AWS/Azure images (passwordless doas to root), is the main exposure, and the flaw is actively exploited and in CISA's KEV catalog. OpenSSH 10.6p2 fixes it.

insights.claim: CVE-2026-123158 (*sshole) lets an unauthenticated attacker log into accounts with no usable password on OpenSSH systems built against musl libc without PAM, by supplying any password between 257 and 1,024 characters.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: A remote auth bypass in SSH is a top-severity exposure for any fleet running Alpine-based or musl builds.
insights.locator: A recently disclosed vulnerability in OpenSSH

insights.claim: For passwords over 256 bytes musl's crypt() returns an asterisk as an error value, the same character /etc/shadow uses to mark no-password accounts, so OpenSSH treats it as a hash match and permits login.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Illustrates how sentinel-value collisions across libraries create critical vulnerabilities, a class auditors should hunt for.
insights.locator: The flaw comes from the way OpenSSH checks

insights.claim: The bug combined two 2012 musl changes (asterisk error return from crypt() and a 256-byte SHA-512 input limit) with a 2016 OpenSSH fix for timing attack CVE-2016-6210 that hashed supplied passwords using another account's salt.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Security fixes can create new vulnerabilities years later; long-tail interaction bugs justify investment in configuration-matrix fuzzing.

insights.claim: The flaw went unnoticed for roughly a decade because OpenSSH is tested on OpenBSD and glibc systems and most distributions route authentication through PAM; it was found by building OpenSSH in several configurations and testing about 17,600 unusual login attempts.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Less-common build configurations (musl, embedded) are under-tested attack surfaces in widely trusted software.
insights.locator: Kultekin writes that the issue remained unnoticed

themes.theme: Exposure: Alpine, cloud images and embedded

insights.claim: Alpine Linux is the most prominent affected distribution because it uses musl and its default OpenSSH configuration does not enable PAM; OpenWrt, Buildroot and Yocto may also be affected, while glibc, PAM, Dropbear and OpenBSD systems are not.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Container and embedded/IoT fleets built on Alpine or musl need immediate inventory; embedded devices may stay unpatched for long periods.
insights.locator: Alpine Linux is the most prominent distribution affected

insights.claim: On Alpine's official AWS and Azure images, the default alpine user is passwordless and has passwordless doas, so exploiting the bug yields root within seconds.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Cloud VMs launched from official Alpine images with internet-facing SSH are effectively root-exposed until patched.
insights.quote: On alpine's official aws and azure images that's the default `alpine` user, and it has passwordless `doas`. so it's root
insights.locator: On Alpine's official AWS and Azure images

insights.claim: Red Hat products and Amazon Linux 2 and 2023 are not affected because they lack the musl-without-PAM combination, but Alpine-based containers, embedded devices and custom musl builds remain at risk.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Risk concentrates in container images and embedded devices rather than mainstream enterprise Linux distributions.
insights.locator: Red Hat has said that its products are not affected

insights.claim: CVE-2026-123158 was disclosed on 5 November 2026, exploitation followed within days, and the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 9 November.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: KEV listing triggers mandatory federal remediation deadlines and typically spikes demand for vulnerability management tooling.
insights.locator: The vulnerability was publicly disclosed on 5 November

insights.claim: GreyNoise reported Southeast Asian honeypots attacked by group GT10 deploying a backdoor for shell commands, reconnaissance and persistence; watchTowr linked activity to botnets and cryptocurrency operations, and Previdian recorded 20 attempts from 13 IPs in nine countries.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Rapid weaponization by botnet/crypto-mining operators shows disclosure-to-exploit windows are now days, favoring automated patching and threat-intel vendors.
insights.locator: The vulnerability is being actively exploited

insights.claim: OpenSSH 10.6p2 fixes CVE-2026-123158; operators unable to update can set PasswordAuthentication no and restart sshd, and should check authentication logs for passwordless accounts accepting passwords.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Disabling password auth is a near-zero-cost mitigation; key-only SSH remains best practice.
